  \item Every $L(M)$ has exactly $3n\binom{n}{4} + I(M)$ tetrahedra, where $I(M)$
        is the number of intercalates (Theorem~\ref{thm:tetra}).
  \item The proposed formulas $n^2(n-1)^2$ (triangles),
        $(n-1)^3 n^2 - 6I(M)$ (tetrahedra), and the derived homology dimension
        $(n-1)^3 - I(M)$ from a vanishing $\partial_3$ are false, and the last two
        mutually inconsistent (Section~\ref{sec:refute}).
  \item We clarify which part of the homological claim survives as an open
        conjecture (Section~\ref{sec:disc}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Definitions}

Throughout $n \geq 2$ and $M$ is a Latin square, meaning each row map
$j \mapsto M_{ij}$ and each column map $i \mapsto M_{ij}$ is a bijection.

\begin{definition}[Latin square graph]
The graph $L(M)$ has vertex set $V = \{(i,j) : 0 \le i,j < n\}$, with distinct
$p=(i,j)$, $q=(k,\ell)$ adjacent iff $i=k$ (same row), $j=\ell$ (same column), or
$M_{ij}=M_{k\ell}$ (same symbol). Each adjacency has a unique \emph{flavor}, and
no adjacent pair has two flavors simultaneously.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Line]
A \emph{line} is a maximal monochromatic clique: one of the $n$ rows, $n$
columns, or $n$ symbol classes. There are $3n$ lines, each an $n$-vertex clique;
two distinct lines meet in at most one vertex.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Clique]
$S \subseteq V$ is a clique if pairwise adjacent; a $k$-clique has $k$ vertices.
In the clique (flag) complex a $k$-clique is a $(k-1)$-simplex.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Intercalate]
An \emph{intercalate} is a $2\times2$ Latin subsquare: rows $i<i'$ and columns
$j<j'$ with $M_{ij}=M_{i'j'}$ and $M_{ij'}=M_{i'j}$ (forcing $M_{ij}\neq M_{ij'}$).
Its count is
\[
I(M) = \#\{(i,i',j,j') : i<i',\ j<j',\ M_{ij}=M_{i'j'},\ M_{ij'}=M_{i'j}\}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Cyclic Latin square]
$C_n$ is defined by $(C_n)_{ij} = i+j \bmod n$. It is Latin for all $n$; $C_5$ is
intercalate-free and $C_4$ has $I(C_4)=4$.
\end{definition}

\section{The triangle count}

\begin{lemma}[Edge-flavor dichotomy for triangles]\label{lem:tri-dich}
Every triangle of $L(M)$ either has all three vertices on a common line, or its
three edges have three distinct flavors.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If two edges share a flavor at a common vertex, say two row edges at $A$, then all
three vertices lie on $A$'s row. Otherwise, with three edges among three flavors,
each flavor occurs once.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Line triangles]\label{lem:tri-line}
The number of line triangles is $3n\binom{n}{3}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Each of the $3n$ lines contributes $\binom{n}{3}$ triangles; two lines share at
most one vertex, so no triangle is double-counted.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Transversal triangles]\label{lem:tri-trans}
The number of transversal triangles is $n^2(n-1)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Summing common neighbors over edges gives
$\sum_e \lambda_e = 3\cdot\#\text{triangles}$ with $\lambda_e = n$ for every edge
and $\#\text{edges} = \tfrac12 n^2\cdot 3(n-1)$, whence
$\#\text{triangles} = \tfrac{n^3(n-1)}{2}$. Subtracting the line count
$3n\binom{n}{3} = \tfrac{n^2(n-1)(n-2)}{2}$ leaves $n^2(n-1)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Triangle count]\label{thm:tri}
For every Latin square $M$ of order $n$,
\[
\#\{\text{triangles of } L(M)\} = 3n\binom{n}{3} + n^2(n-1) = \frac{n^3(n-1)}{2},
\]
independent of $M$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Add Lemmas~\ref{lem:tri-line} and~\ref{lem:tri-trans}; the families are disjoint
by Lemma~\ref{lem:tri-dich}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$L(C_5)$ has $\tfrac{5^3\cdot4}{2}=250$ triangles, confirmed by direct
enumeration.
\end{corollary}

\section{The tetrahedron count}

\begin{lemma}[Edge-flavor dichotomy for tetrahedra]\label{lem:tetra-dich}
Every $4$-clique of $L(M)$ either has all four vertices on a common line, or is
the vertex set of an intercalate.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If some vertex meets two edges of one flavor, those force a line, and iterating
yields a line tetrahedron. Otherwise the four vertices are not contained in a
line, and tracking the Latin constraints forces the configuration
$\{(i,j),(i,j'),(i',j),(i',j')\}$ with $M_{ij}=M_{i'j'}$ and $M_{ij'}=M_{i'j}$,
an intercalate. Conversely each intercalate's four cells are pairwise adjacent
(two row, two column, two symbol edges), hence a $4$-clique.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Line tetrahedra]\label{lem:tetra-line}
The number of line tetrahedra is $3n\binom{n}{4}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Each of the $3n$ lines contributes $\binom{n}{4}$; distinct lines share at most
one vertex, so there is no overlap.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tetrahedron count]\label{thm:tetra}
For every Latin square $M$ of order $n$,
\[
\#\{K_4 \text{ of } L(M)\} = 3n\binom{n}{4} + I(M).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:tetra-dich} the $4$-cliques split into disjoint line and
intercalate families. Lemma~\ref{lem:tetra-line} counts the first; the second is
in bijection with intercalates.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$I(C_5)=0$, so $L(C_5)$ has $3\cdot5\cdot\binom54=75$ tetrahedra;
$I(C_4)=4$, so $L(C_4)$ has $3\cdot4\cdot\binom44+4=16$. Both confirmed by
enumeration.
\end{corollary}

\section{Refutation of the proposed formulas}\label{sec:refute}

A prior proposal asserted, for $n\ge 5$: (T1) triangle count $n^2(n-1)^2$;
(T2) tetrahedron count $(n-1)^3 n^2 - 6I(M)$; (T3) $\operatorname{rank}
\partial_3 = 6I(M)$ with a vanishing-boundary reading giving second homology
$(n-1)^3 - I(M)$.

\begin{proposition}[T1 false]
For $C_5$ the true triangle count is $250$, while $n^2(n-1)^2 = 400$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[T2 false]
For $C_5$ the true tetrahedron count is $75$, while
$(n-1)^3 n^2 - 6I(M) = 1600$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[T3 false and inconsistent with T2]
Over $\FF_2$ (admissible for $C_5$ since the characteristic does not divide $5$),
the third boundary map $\partial_3$ of the clique complex of $L(C_5)$ is nonzero,
so $\operatorname{rank}\partial_3 \geq 1$. But (T3) with $I(C_5)=0$ forces
$\operatorname{rank}\partial_3 = 0$, a contradiction.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
$L(C_5)$ contains a tetrahedron $\sigma$ (indeed $75$). Over $\FF_2$,
$\partial_3\sigma$ is the sum of its four distinct triangular faces, hence
nonzero. Thus $\partial_3 \neq 0$. This is the internal inconsistency: (T2)
demands many top simplices while (T3) demands their boundaries vanish.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The correct intercalate correction is \emph{additive} ($+I(M)$, Theorem
\ref{thm:tetra}), whereas (T2) subtracts $6I(M)$. Intercalates create tetrahedra.
\end{remark}

\section{Discussion: what survives about the homology}\label{sec:disc}

The refutation dismantles the derivation of $\dim H_2 = (n-1)^3 - I(M)$ but not
the target value. Two points stand. First, the shortcut is dead: $H_2$ cannot be
read off with a zero $\partial_3$, since $\partial_3\neq0$. Second, the corrected
face vector
\[
(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3) = \Big(n^2,\ \tfrac32 n^2(n-1),\ \tfrac{n^3(n-1)}{2},\
3n\tbinom{n}{4}+I(M)\Big)
\]
gives a sound basis for Euler-characteristic and rank computations, and $I(M)$ is
the only face count that varies among squares of fixed order. Thus $\dim H_2 =
(n-1)^3 - I(M)$ is best treated as an open conjecture resting on these corrected
inputs.

\section{Future work}

Field-independence (torsion-freeness) of the clique homology; extremal topology
(do intercalate-free squares maximize the second Betti number?); general-$n$
proofs of Theorems~\ref{thm:tri} and~\ref{thm:tetra}; and higher cliques, where
no transversal $K_5$ exists so only line cliques survive.

\section{Conclusion}

Cliques of $L(M)$ are either monochromatic (on a line) or built from all three
edge flavors. This yields a square-independent triangle count
$\tfrac{n^3(n-1)}{2}$ and a tetrahedron count $3n\binom{n}{4}+I(M)$ isolating the
intercalate number, while refuting a trio of appealing but incorrect formulas.
The precise second homology remains open, now on correct combinatorial
foundations.

**Conjecture.** The Betti numbers of the clique complex of a Latin square graph are
independent of the coefficient field; equivalently, its integral homology is
torsion-free in degrees up to two.

small threshold, and their asymptotic density is now understood, so the two ends of
the spectrum can be exhibited explicitly and compared.

closed invariant of the Latin square, and how it relates to the intercalate count
and to isotopy class, remains to be explored.

from math import comb
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple

Cell = Tuple[int, int]
Square = Callable[[int, int], int]


def cyclic_square(n: int) -> Square:
    """The cyclic Latin square of order n: M(i, j) = (i + j) mod n."""
    return lambda i, j: (i + j) % n


def is_latin(M: Square, n: int) -> bool:
    """Check that every row and every column of M is a permutation of 0..n-1."""
    for i in range(n):
        if len({M(i, j) for j in range(n)}) != n:
            return False
    for j in range(n):
        if len({M(i, j) for i in range(n)}) != n:
            return False
    return True

    """All n^2 cells (row, column) of the grid."""
    return [(i, j) for i in range(n) for j in range(n)]


def adjacent(M: Square, p: Cell, q: Cell) -> bool:
    """Adjacency in the Latin square graph: shared row, column, or symbol."""
    (i, j), (k, l) = p, q
    return i == k or j == l or M(i, j) == M(k, l)

    """Whether the cells in S are pairwise adjacent."""
    return all(adjacent(M, S[a], S[b]) for a in range(len(S)) for b in range(a + 1, len(S)))


def count_cliques(M: Square, n: int, k: int) -> int:
    """Brute-force count of k-vertex cliques of L(M)."""
